messages.body_plain:
Dear Omar,

I tried your plethodon example and had no issue.  Based on the configuration you have, the issue might be that the Matrix library is not up-to-date.  The Matrix library (now version 1.7-0) was updated, requiring R >= 4.4.0, and because geomorph and RRPP depend on Matrix, we also had to require R >= 4.4.0 in most recent versions.  However, it looks like it is possible to retain an older version of Matrix without triggering a warning to update it.   Note that “order" is an argument in several Matrix functions (at least the new version), and we do set it to 0 in one of the new RRPP functions (QRforX), so the probability that the error is caused by the out-of-date Matrix library is probably high.

If I were you, I would update Matrix, restart R, and see if the issue persists.

Best,
Mike

As a follow-up, I checked the NEWS for the Matrix library.  The “New Features” for version 1.6-1 (August 2023) had the following news note:

The lu and qr methods for class dgCMatrix now admit an order argument with value in 0:3, allowing the expert user to choose among all ordering methods made available by the CSparse library.
So it seems reasonable that Matrix 1.4-1 (Only current as of March 2022) would have trouble using an argument that does not exist in the function.  I would now say the probability that the issue lies with your version of Matrix is 99.9%.

- Mike

** Read below only if you are a coding geek!

Regarding the bolded text above, for “the expert user” who might be following this thread, being able to choose the ordering method in a QR decomposition is a HUGE development.  For very large linear model design matrices — the kind one might have in a bilateral symmetry analysis or a measurement error analysis — it was previously impossible to have dense-matrix qr and sparse-matrix qr find commensurate results when there were redundant parameters in the matrix (common with nested designs).  Previously, we had to coerce sparse matrices into dense matrices to remove dimensions — a process that might take longer than all of the RRPP iterations for calculating SS thousands of times — then coerce the dense matrix back to a sparse matrix to take advantage of sparse-matrix algebra for fast computations.  We no longer have to do this because changing the order method for removing redundant parameters means we can now have commensurate sparse- and dense-matrix approaches.  While this might not feel like news because it changes nothing, it is actually really important (and it actually changes a lot, other than results).  Here is a demo (noting that vegan::adonis does not take advantage of sparse-matrix algebra):

Mihajlo

messages.subject_clean: Advice on Workflow for Asymmetry Analysis Using bilat.symmetry in Triatomines
messages.body_plain:
Dear Geomorph community,

I hope this message finds you well. I would like to ask about the correct workflow for analyzing asymmetry using the bilat.symmetry function in geomorph. Specifically, I aim to study whether there are changes in wing asymmetry of triatomines associated with three levels of anthropization (high, intermediate, low). My data include two species (Triatoma garciabesi and Triatoma guasayana) and both sexes (males and females). Previous studies have shown the presence of sexual dimorphism in morphological traits of triatomines, and both species have structures with different shapes.

My question is: would it be better to perform the analysis using the complete dataset or to separate it by species and sex? In the first case, I assume that the mean shape would be calculated from the combined shape changes of both species and sexes. In the second case, I believe it might yield more accurate results in terms of shape changes by sex and species.

I would appreciate your advice on this approach.

Thank you for your time and help!

Best regards,

Federico Fiad

Federico,

Any GM study requires a common GPA prior to downstream tests or analyses. The common GPA, which is part of bilat.symmetry, ensures that all objects are aligned in common and reside in the same tangent space. Doing separate GPA will not do that.

Once a common GPA is performed, one may then subset the data for any specific analyses that are question-specific.

Dean

Dear Daniel et al.,

I have updated RRPP::summary.pairwise to include “stdist” as an option for comparison of slope vectors.  You can install RRPP from Github and the your analysis should work now.  I have not yet updated the Mahalanobis distance option (“mdist”) but that is up next.  Although I made this update, I do so with a little trepidation.

The reason for my trepidation is that I am not comfortable with the multivariate generalization that is inherently assumed.  For example, with parametric multi-mean comparisons, there are different statistics that can be used but one is a pairwise t-statistic that looks a two-sample t-statistic for independent samples, substituting the MSE from a linear model for the pooled variance from two independent samples.  Either the “stdist” or “mdist” options are multivariate generalizations of this concept, using the trace or the determinant of the MSE matrix, respectively.

There is similarly a two-sample t-statistic for comparing slopes from independent regressions.  This statistic looks just like the two-sample t-statistic for independent means, substituting slopes for means.  But I don’t really know of an analogous pairwise slopes test in an ANOVA or MANOVA framework using t-statistics substituting MSE for pooled variance of slopes.  I believe the reason for this is probably a practical matter.  If one were to attempt to perform an ANCOVA and learn there is heterogeneity among slopes, they would probably be compelled to perform different linear regressions by group, and subsequently compare slopes with two-sample t-tests for slopes.

Therefore, I am making the assumption that (1) because a pairwise t-test for means substitutes MSE for pooled variance from independent samples, and (2) the pooled variance between independent samples for slopes has the same calculation as between means, then (3) it makes sense to calculate the pooled SE for a “stdist” test comparing slopes with the MSE matrix from a linear model that contains parameters for a group factor and covariate, plus interaction.  Furthermore, because coefficients for slopes and means are basically the same thing in a linear model — the numerator in the standardized distance is based on the cross-product of a vector that is the difference between vectors of coefficients — the “stdist” calculation applied to either slopes or means is mathematically commensurate.

I cannot find a reason this logic is flawed but it could be because I am missing something obvious.  I am willing to take the chance because of the first principle soundness of calculation.  Hopefully I am not missing something!

Hope this works for you!
Mike

Hi Federico,

I just wanted to add a perspective here regarding your locality data.

If you have GPS coordinates and can estimate geographical distances among sites, it might be preferable to use the geographic distance matrix as input to the model in the form of a covariance matrix (use the Cov = argument in procD.lm) representing how you think covariation in your shapes is structured among sites.

If you choose to use this approach, you might find cov.spatial in the geoR library useful, where you can specify if covariance between localities decays with distance following different functions (a Gaussian, exponential, etc.).

Best,
Bryan

I have not yet updated the Mahalanobis distance option (“mdist”) but that is up next.  Although I made this update, I do so with a little trepidation.
>
> The reason for my trepidation is that I am not comfortable with the multivariate generalization that is inherently assumed.  For example, with parametric multi-mean comparisons, there are different statistics that can be used but one is a pairwise t-statistic that looks a two-sample t-statistic for independent samples, substituting the MSE from a linear model for the pooled variance from two independent samples.  Either the “stdist” or “mdist” options are multivariate generalizations of this concept, using the trace or the determinant of the MSE matrix, respectively.
>
> There is similarly a two-sample t-statistic for comparing slopes from independent regressions.  This statistic looks just like the two-sample t-statistic for independent means, substituting slopes for means.  But I don’t really know of an analogous pairwise slopes test in an ANOVA or MANOVA framework using t-statistics substituting MSE for pooled variance of slopes.  I believe the reason for this is probably a practical matter.  If one were to attempt to perform an ANCOVA and learn there is heterogeneity among slopes, they would probably be compelled to perform different linear regressions by group, and subsequently compare slopes with two-sample t-tests for slopes.
>
> Therefore, I am making the assumption that (1) because a pairwise t-test for means substitutes MSE for pooled variance from independent samples, and (2) the pooled variance between independent samples for slopes has the same calculation as between means, then (3) it makes sense to calculate the pooled SE for a “stdist” test comparing slopes with the MSE matrix from a linear model that contains parameters for a group factor and covariate, plus interaction.  Furthermore, because coefficients for slopes and means are basically the same thing in a linear model — the numerator in the standardized distance is based on the cross-product of a vector that is the difference between vectors of coefficients — the “stdist” calculation applied to either slopes or means is mathematically commensurate.
>
> I cannot find a reason this logic is flawed but it could be because I am missing something obvious.  I am willing to take the chance because of the first principle soundness of calculation.  Hopefully I am not missing something!
